📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there's no denying Andrew Scott delivered one of the most compelling portrayals of Moriarty opposite Benedict Cumberbatch in what remains one of the standout adaptations of Sherlock Holmes. The show ran on the BBC for 4 seasons, and fans are still holding out hope for a 5th run. I honestly thought this would be the role he was most recognized for, but it turns out that's not the case. Without hesitation, Scott told me it's actually the “Hot Priest” from Fleabag.

During a recent interview with CinemaBlend for his upcoming film Elsinore, which I think is one of the best films on the 2026 movie schedule, Scott spoke about portraying Ian Charleson, who is best known for his role in Chariots of Fire. I had to ask him which of his own roles he is most recognized for, and he didn't skip a beat:.

Recent findings suggest that hot priest. Yeah, it's Fleabag usually. Maybe a bit of Ripley, a bit of Sherlock. A lot of the thing, because of NT [National Theatre] Live, which is a theater platform. Vanya is a play that I did, and a lot of people have seen it because of that platform… And that's the thing. Or else they just - they just don't; they just avoid me like, 'Oh, there's a dodgy person.'.

I'm glad to see I'm not alone in this. For me, and clearly for a lot more people than I thought, Scott is the ‘Hot Priest.' He takes a man of the cloth and makes him layered, complicated, charismatic, and, above all, very sexy. If you've seen Fleabag, I'm sure the line “Kneel. Just kneel.” is burned into your brain for all eternity, just like it is mine. He clearly has a knack for making even a single line stick with audiences, as is the case with his one line in Saving Private Ryan.

It has been revealed that scott has a way of making normally unsexy professions seem sexy, all while making even a single line incredibly memorable. Recently, he was a guest star on a show called It Gets Worse, where he plays a therapist, so I had to ask him if people might start calling him 'Hot Therapist' now. Both he and Billie Piper weighed in.

Piper is spot on. I watched it, and there is no other word to describe that scene. But Scott is so much more than "hot." He is, in my opinion, a once-in-a-generation talent, and the roles he plays are memorable. He has this rare ability to make even the biggest performances feel incredibly personal, almost like he's speaking directly to each individual person watching. That's especially true in Elsinore. I think he's going to give Robert Pattinson a run for his money this Oscar season. Honest.

In a recent development, I'm sure people will continue to call Scott 'Hot Priest,' and he'll, of course, still be recognized as Moriarty when they see him. I secretly hope he gets 'Hot Therapist' thrown out occasionally now, too. With Elsinore hitting theaters on December 4, I have a feeling audiences might soon have another role to associate him with. And honestly, after this performance, I'd be surprised if Ian Charleson and Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, didn't start topping that list.

Industry observers note that tasha Suri, author of the Burning Kingdoms trilogy and several other books, will be writing Baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart, the official BG3books website has announced. Another prequel to Larian's videogame, this one focuses on Shadowheart's time as a priestess in the Church of Shar, and is about a murder mystery.

Sources indicate that "When a member of their order is killed in the Upper City," the blurb goes, "Shadowheart and her so-called allies are called to investigate. She trusts none of them: not Mirie, the ambitious Griefguard; not Caldan, the cynical propagandist; and certainly not Nocturne, the charming quartermistress, who claims to have only Shadowheart’s best interests in mind.".

It has been revealed that mirie and Nocturne are both characters you can meet in Baldur's Gate 3, while Caldan Darkwood is mentioned in a note you can find. Nocturne in particular has a close relationship with Shadowheart, which could be interesting to see developed. "Torn between the familiar comforts of the dark and the thrill of fresh desire," the blurb continues, "she must solve the mystery to prove her devotion… or be cast into the light.".

Which sounds fine and dandy, but it'll have an uphill battle with the Baldur's Gate 3 fandom, who've been vocally critical of the Astarion novel for its lightness of tone—especially given his traumatic backstory—and apparently mischaracterizing Astarion and his sire, Cazador, as well as being inaccurate to the lore.

I haven't read the Astarion book, but I did read the original Baldur's Gate novels, which were terrible. So were almost all the D&D books I read in a youthful post-Tolkien haze where I'd put up with anything that had wizards in it. My expectations are pretty low, but I do like to slip a trashy fantasy novel between heavier reads as a palate-cleanser so maybe I'll try this one some day.

Baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart will be out in a 304-page hardcover edition and in ebook form on June 8, as well as a 10-hour audiobook. The Astarion audiobook was read by Astarion performer Neil Newbon, we'll have to wait and see if Jennifer English reads the Shadowheart book.

If the series continues I could see a Wyll prequel being interesting, since he gets a bit short-changed in the videogame, though I wouldn't expect it to sell as well as novels about the more popular companions.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At 6:04 on the morning of March 29, 2024, my phone lit up with a long text from Matt Rutledge.
  • I was a few weeks out from my partnership interview at a New York law firm.
  • Recent findings suggest that he had spent years teaching me to use his word for it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At 6:04 on the morning of March 29, 2024, my phone lit up with a long text from Matt Rutledge. The head of school had called him the night before, he wrote, while he was watching television with his wife. He was on paid administrative leave, his school email was frozen, and he assumed this was about him and me. He called what he had done to me a relationship. He didn’t regret his feelings for me. Could I call him when his wife was out of the house?

I was thirty-seven years old. I was a few weeks out from my partnership interview at a New York law firm. I had a husband and a three-year-old son. I spend my working life telling clients which sentences will look bad in discovery. I read that text twice, and my first thought was, How can I help him?

Recent findings suggest that he had spent years teaching me to use his word for it. It was never a relationship. He groomed me, he exploited me, and he raped me.

Industry observers note that vanity Fair has written about that morning before. Evgenia Peretz opened “Girls, Interrupted” with that text in January 2025, and she went back to Miss Hall’s last fall after the investigation came out. In March, Dan Adler covered the indictment. This time I’m telling it myself.

It has been revealed that later that morning an email arrived from an attorney in Boston. Subject line: “Reaching out about Miss Hall’s School.” I didn’t open it right away. I didn’t need to. Some part of me had been composing that email in my head since I was a teenager. The attorney represented a woman named Melissa Fares, a Miss Hall’s alumna who had been there a few years after me. I had never heard her name.

She had heard mine. Years earlier, older girls at the school had told her about me. She held on to my name, and when she went to a lawyer she remembered it. By then I had married and changed it, and they found me anyway.

I called Matt and asked. “Who is Melissa?” There was a pause long enough to hear him decide something, then a sigh, and then he told me he had had sex with Melissa while she was a student.

Here is what I did next, and I’d ask you to withhold judgment. I told him I would call the lawyer, find out what she had, and report back.

Sources indicate that that’s what twenty-two years of being groomed looks like at a desk in Midtown. You don’t make a decision. The decision was made for you a long time ago, in a dorm room, and you’re simply carrying it out.

I did call the lawyer. And when I heard my own voice say “I’m not ready to talk to you, I want to talk to Melissa,” I think that was the first sentence in two decades that I stated entirely for myself.

Sources indicate that melissa called that afternoon. I don’t remember how she started. I remember what I said before she got far.

“I’ve been waiting for your call for twenty years.”.

Recent findings suggest that I meant it literally. Some part of me had always known I wasn’t the only one. I just couldn’t go looking. I could only wait to be found.

Hilary Simon and Melissa Fares, photographed in Far Rockaway, Newly introduced York, 2025.

She told me her story, and I heard my own memories come out of a stranger’s mouth. He called her “Little One.” He called me “Little One.” He took her to the same hotel in Northampton. He told her he would kill himself if she ever told anyone, which is a thing he had also told me, more than once, in nearly the same words. He had made himself the center of her emotional world before he ever touched her. He had a script.

For twenty years he had me believing that what happened was singular, and that it was my fault. By the end of that call it was a pattern, and I was a data point. I was not special. It is a strange thing to grieve, not being special to the person who hurt you. I grieved it anyway.

After more than three decades teaching at that school, he resigned the same day.

According to recent reports, I arrived at Miss Hall’s, an all-girls boarding school in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, in the fall of 2001. I was fourteen, homesick, and like every other girl my age, positive I was more grown up than I was.

Rutledge had been teaching history there for a decade. He was a major man with a booming voice, married with two daughters. He lived with his family in a school-owned house across the street from the main entrance. He used to cut the lunch line announcing himself as “Mr. Wonderful.” Girls talked about him like he was a minor deity. They also mentioned, in the breezy way teenagers mention terrible things, that he had a type.

Some evenings, he was one of the adults who did bed checks in the dorms. The others always stood in the doorway. He came in and sat on the edge of my bed.

In a recent development, by the next fall he was my advisor and my cross-country coach. There was no door at that school he couldn’t open. On the long drives to meets, he told me to sit next to him in the school van. He called me his copilot. The rest of the team sat behind us. He would put his hand on my upper thigh, or pull me close until our legs were touching. I watched the Berkshire hills go by and tried not to look down.

That was the first line he crossed. I was fifteen. After that he crossed them one at a time until there were none left. He kept abusing me for years after I graduated.

From the outside, those years looked like a success story.

According to recent reports, I went to college and then law school. I became a civil defense attorney. I got married. I had a son. I was good at my job.

Sources indicate that I could find the unanswered email in ten thousand pages of discovery. The report nobody followed up on. I couldn’t open my own file.

When I tell this story, people ask me some version of the same question. How did nobody notice?

Industry observers note that in the late 1990s, years before I ever set foot on Miss Hall’s campus, a student stood up at a school meeting and said Mr. Rutledge was having sex with another student. The school suspended her for the rest of the year, barred her from graduation and made her write him an apology letter. He kept teaching.

According to recent reports, on my graduation day, Rutledge kissed me and told me that he loved me. A classmate told a staff member, who reported it to the administration. In a memo, Rutledge admitted telling me he loved me but said “[it was] not a romantic expression.” He denied the kiss. They took his word for it. No one called me or my parents.

Hilary Simon on graduation day.

Sources indicate that A few years later, after a family reported that he had made advances toward their daughter, the head of school at that time, Jeannie Norris, put a warning to Rutledge in writing. “This isn’t the 70s or the 80s,” she wrote. “Society has no stomach for any kind of inappropriate behavior between adults and girls or teachers and students.” She was worried about the school’s reputation, and about his. In the letter she stated the incident had “the potential for seriously damaging the School and your [Rutledge’s] reputation.” He was not fired.

Over the years that followed Rutledge was made chair of the history department and collected faculty honors. More than one person gave the school my name as a girl he had singled out. Nobody ever called me. In June 2023, I heard another alumna tried to raise concerns about him with the head of school at that time. He was still teaching nine months later, when Melissa reported him.

Recent findings suggest that in August 2025 Miss Hall’s published the results of an outside investigation it had commissioned from Aleta Law. The investigators substantiated grooming and abuse by Rutledge involving at least five students. They found school leadership had been warned about him over the years and hadn’t acted. Staff members told investigators they had suspected him and kept quiet, some because they feared retaliation, others because they assumed no one in charge would listen.

Industry observers note that it went beyond Rutledge. The investigation found that seven other Miss Hall’s employees had engaged in sexual misconduct with students, dating back to the 1940s. Eight adults across eighty plus years. That’s a culture of abuse.

A Berkshire County grand jury has since indicted Norris on a charge of reckless endangerment of a child. She has pleaded not guilty. Another former Miss Hall’s teacher has been indicted for assault with intent to rape and indecent assault and two counts battery of a student. He has also pleaded not guilty.

I read all sixty pages of the Aleta Law report in one sitting. Nothing in it surprised me. It still knocked the air out of me to see my adolescence reduced to numbered findings.

Melissa arrived at Miss Hall’s in 2007, two years after I left.

It has been revealed that people sometimes call us friends. That’s true, but it’s a small word for it. I call her my sister survivor.

I wouldn’t be writing this if Melissa hadn’t gone first. She went to the school alone. In April 2024, she told her story publicly. A few weeks later, I told mine. Then other women came forward. They noted Rutledge had abused them too.

In October 2024, the Berkshire district attorney said he didn’t believe he could charge Rutledge. In Massachusetts, the age of consent is sixteen. Under the law, a teacher could claim that a sixteen- or seventeen-year-old student had consented.

Industry observers note that melissa and I set out to change the law. We testified at the State House and knocked on every door that would open. Enough Abuse, a Massachusetts nonprofit, had been fighting for this for years. Two national advocacy groups, World Without Exploitation and I Have The Right To, stood with us. Representatives Leigh Davis and John Lawn pushed for it in the House, and Senator Joan Lovely added it to the state budget. In July, Governor Healey signed the Trusted Adults Act.

In Massachusetts, it is now a felony for a teacher or coach to have sex with a student under eighteen.

Melissa and I spoke at the signing ceremony. I stood right next to the governor and thought about the girl in the front seat of the school van, with her teacher’s hand on her leg.

While we were working on the law, Massachusetts State Police and a new team of prosecutors in the Berkshire district attorney’s office had reopened the investigation into Rutledge. Melissa and I testified before a grand jury. In March, he was indicted on three counts of rape.

In a recent development, in April, he was arraigned. It was the first time Melissa and I faced him together. In the courtroom, I handed out orange heart stickers. Orange is Melissa’s favorite color. When we saw Rutledge, we both went numb. We had learned to do that as girls, when going somewhere else in our heads was the only way through. He pleaded not guilty.

I looked back at the benches. They were full of orange. Teachers from Miss Hall’s, people from the community, alumnae across generations. I had been alone with this since I was fifteen. That day, a whole room sat behind us. Afterward, Melissa told reporters that for the first time, she held the power in a room with him. I felt it too.

According to recent reports, this month, nine years after #MeToo took off, a jury in London convicted Russell Brand of one rape and three sexual assaults. A judge sentenced him to ten and a half years in prison. His crimes went back to 2004. Brand’s attorneys argued the women had waited too long to be believed. I waited twenty years. Delay is often the most ordinary fact in these cases.

Industry observers note that in the midterms, Ohio elected Amy Acton governor. A few weeks before the vote, her opponent’s campaign ran an ad in which her estranged mother called her a liar. Acton’s stepfather had been charged with raping her when she was a child. Republicans and Democrats both condemned the ad. She won anyway.

I watched the returns on election night and thought about the girls at Miss Hall’s who told the truth and were called liars. Survivors get called liars all the time. We almost never get to watch one win.

Sources indicate that tarana Burke knew survivors weren’t being believed long before most people were listening. She started saying “me too” in 2006 to reach Black girls who had survived sexual violence, more than ten years before it became a hashtag. Every survivor who spoke after her made it a little easier for the next one.

In a recent development, in November 2024, a Cornell student told campus police and the Title IX office that she had been gang-raped at a fraternity house weeks earlier. No one has been charged. Cornell’s president set up a task force on sexual assault, but he later admitted he never checked how her case ended.

When I read that, I was back at Miss Hall’s on graduation day, waiting for a phone call that nobody made.

Industry observers note that the Epstein survivors know that silence too. For decades, powerful people looked away. Last year survivors pushed Congress to pass a law requiring the Justice Department to release its Epstein files. Millions of pages came out. There have been no arrests in the United States.

It has been revealed that I’m still hopeful. Survivors everywhere keep coming forward, and some of the people in charge are finally acting. My body knew what Rutledge had done to me long before I let myself say it aloud. I didn’t have the words. Survivors today do, and they have each other. Melissa found me.

Industry observers note that the criminal case against Rutledge isn’t over. His lawyer has asked a judge to dismiss all charges. We don’t know yet whether there will be a trial. Whatever the judge decides, I’ve already reached my own verdict. I’m healing and Rutledge doesn’t get a say in that.

Sources indicate that for most of my life, I carried shame that was never mine. He handed it to me. Every adult who looked away handed me a little more.

Predators don’t work alone. Someone always sees something. In the movie Spotlight, a lawyer indicates that if it takes a village to raise a child, it takes a village to abuse one. My village saw. The people in charge did nothing.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve given the shame back. It belongs to him, and to the people who could have stopped him.

If you are a survivor and you are still carrying shame, you can put it down.

In a recent development, borrow my courage if you need it. Melissa lent me hers.

Neither Matthew Rutledge nor Jean Norris responded to Vanity Fair for the original story, and neither of them has made direct statements to the press. Norris, through her attorney, claimed not to know that Rutledge abused students.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I am both a bit too young and a bit too very not American to have ever experienced public-access television, but it's something that's always fascinated me. For those too young to have even heard of it, or just not in the know, it essentially allowed anyone to broadcast their own indicates through cable TV. A proto YouTube, if you will. It's obviously not what it was any more, given the advent of the internet, but in NIGHTEYE.TV, it may be making a digital, more interactive return.

NIGHTEYE.TV is a strange little place. I call it a place, it's a fake TV floating in a Unity default texture void, lending it a Backroomsian vibe, but even if there's not much there to ground yourself in, the goggle box is enticing all the same. It beckons you to turn it on, a series of buttons all linking to different "channels." What awaits you isn't television, however. Instead you'll find games, mostly of the weirdo, freako, sicko variety, rapidly setting the tone.

🌕NIGHT EYE TV’s initial form is live!🌑 Check out the site and follow our Indiegogo campaign at www.nighteye.tv![image or embed].

Recent findings suggest that in its current incarnation, it's mostly just a collection of clips of these various art games, with direct links to them hidden away in a menu, but a good collection it is. You'll find Nathalie Lawhead's Everything is Going to Be OK, Jeremy Couillard's more recent Soul Injector Commando, and Taylor McCue's He Fucked The Girl Out Of Me. Some clips are longer than others, acting as sort of segments of playthroughs, but it all feels like an exciting evolution of what public-access television was.

Sources indicate that the ultimate goal is for it to be a curated platform where you can buy a rotating selection of games. Most of the sale goes back to the original artist, and 15% gets put into a community pool to be split amongst all of the contributors, with the last 15% going towards keeping everything running. As it stands, that's not quite ready yet. You can help make it happen, though, as right now an Indiegogo campaign is running to help it all get fully operational. Worth chucking a few quid I reckon!

Does GTA 6 have an 'easy mode'? Not officially, but there are two very notable settings you can change to make the game less difficult

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, by now, you've probably heard that you cannot use cheats in GTA 6 until you complete the main story.
  • According to recent reports, but, for anyone looking to have a slightly easier time with GTA 6 than the dev's intended experience, I come with good news: you can make the game a little bit easier by toggling two options in the game's Settings menu.
  • 'Accessible Combat' decreases enemy health and makes them deal less damage to your character — the kind of rebalancing that you'd expect from a traditional difficulty slider.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, by now, you've probably heard that you cannot use cheats in GTA 6 until you complete the main story. Not only that, but enabling cheat codes also locks story progression and deactivates the ability to save. Basically, you can use cheats to have a quick crime spree and blow off some steam, then it's back to normalcy. Understandably, some gamers are a little put out with this change.

According to recent reports, but, for anyone looking to have a slightly easier time with GTA 6 than the dev's intended experience, I come with good news: you can make the game a little bit easier by toggling two options in the game's Settings menu. If you open Settings, and then navigate to Gameplay, you'll find 'Accessible Combat' and 'Reduced Vehicle Damage' toggles. You can activate both to make GTA 6's more difficult elements a little bit easier to work through.

'Accessible Combat' decreases enemy health and makes them deal less damage to your character — the kind of rebalancing that you'd expect from a traditional difficulty slider. 'Reduced Vehicle Damage', as you'd expect, lowers the damage taken by your vehicle and allows your ride to endure more punishment. This applies to gunfire, environmental threats, and impact damage.

Toggle these settings comes with a warning from Rockstar, though. A prompt notes that enabling these modifiers will "significantly change the balance and experience of the gameplay". I've been playing around with these settings and whilst they are not a foolproof 'God Mode' by any means, you can absolutely see a difference in the game when they're enabled: Jason and Lucia take a lot more punishment from melee damage and gunshots, and I had to really try to get Jason's old banged up pickup into even the 'slightly smoking' bracket of disrepair. Your mileage may vary, but these settings, from what I can tell so far, certainly do make the game easier.

Given that cheats disable trophies and progression, these settings might be something to keep in mind if you're trying to find a smoother path through the main story of GTA 6. It's a credit to Rockstar's accessibility teams that these have been included at all - alongside the 23 other gameplay accessibility options, the 12 display options, the 70 UI options, the 24 camera options, and the 14 audio options.

According to recent reports, "We create inclusive, intuitive, and immersive experiences for every player," noted Rockstar's associate UI director, Sam Grosset, in materials provided to Eurogamer ahead of the game's launch. "Accessibility is considered from the outset, and designing for diverse needs enables us to create better games for everyone. We wanted every player in GTA 6 to have options to play the game how they like. Whether it's selecting a larger font size, opting for a more minimal screen experience, or making a controls tweak to sprinting... the choices are open to all.".

We also learned yesterday that Rockstar has made GTA 6 missions "harder to fail" by making them more open-ended, and giving players more ways to figure out how to do things in their own way.

If you need a hand with any of the myriad things GTA 6 asks you to do, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the final weeks of Dancing with the Stars always feature really tough eliminations. However, the last few on the 2026 TV schedule have been brutal. Specifically, Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson went home during the semifinals after getting perfect scores for their Paso Doble and Glee-themed Quickstep. Now, co-host Alfonso Ribeiro has opened up about the conversation he had with the pair following their shocking elimination, and I'm feeling emotional all over again.

In a recent development, while Jenna and Harry were always at the top of the leaderboard and felt like frontrunners on DWTS Season 35, clearly, the fans wanted the other couples in the finale more. During a conversation with TV Insider, Ribeiro shared his thoughts on this, and the conversation he had with the pro and Glee actor after they found out they’d be going home. He stated:.

Industry observers note that there was a lot of sharing of disappointment in my heart, what they did right, and just letting them know that I care and that I’m saddened for them. Or with them. I’ll leave it at that.

I’m also saddened for them. While Harry and Jenna always had some of the best routines of every episode, their DWTS journey was plagued by some controversy and intense online discourse. Of course, there was liftgate, which led to a comment from Johnson’s husband and fellow pro Val Chmerkovskiy that got him suspended from the show for a week. There was also the ongoing debate regarding the amount of dance experience Harry Shum Jr. had before doing DWTS.

However, while Jenna and Harry’s elimination hurt, and Ribeiro spent time talking with them about it, he also noted that no matter what the outcome, the last elimination was going to be painful. It’s the last one before the finale; it would have been heartbreaking no matter who got sent home, as he stated:.

It has been revealed that going into the night, we know that all six of them … we’re going to break hearts with one going home. It wouldn’t have mattered whose name was called. There’d be controversy. There would be, ‘This is a shocking elimination.’ It was going to be that the last several weeks, no matter what, because this for the first time, I think in this show’s history, there were eight people who ultimately could win this show this season for many different reasons. And that’s not normally the case.

It has been revealed that it does feel like the mirrorball trophy could be anyone's. They’re all pretty good, and it’s clear that everyone left has a very devoted fan base. So, it’s unclear who will win, and an argument can be made for any of them. I mean, when I think about all this, there’s part of me that wants Amber Glenn to win, and thinks she can do it based on her scores and consistency. Meanwhile, Connor Wood’s social media likes prove he has a very devoted group of fans behind him that could help make up for his lower scores and push him across the finish line. Seriously, it’s anyone’s game.

So, it made sense that Ribeiro remarked this in the wake of Jenna and Harry’s elimination:.

Industry observers note that there’s ultimate shock every time the person’s name comes up on that card, and also a bit of sadness. Because regardless of who you might think [should go] on and any of that, the reality is that they’ve all put their heart and soul into doing this. They put their lives and their families … they put it all on the back burner while trying to deliver these performances.

Recent findings suggest that I totally see his point. DWTS is a massive time commitment, and it’s an intense experience both physically and mentally. These stars put their everything into it, and so it’s sad to see any of them not reach the end.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Recent findings suggest that however, at the end of the day, this is a competition, and ultimately only one couple can win. To see who takes home the mirrorball, you can catch the finale of Dancing with the Stars this Tuesday, November 24, on ABC or with a Disney+ subscription at 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, as it will air live on both coasts.

ORIGINAL STORY 3PM GMT: Rockstar has finally announced the full cast list for Grand Theft Auto 6, having left fans speculating right up to the game's release about which actors play the game's leads.

Lucia's actor Manni L. Perez was revealed through her nomination for The Game Awards, and it nearly took a photo taken by Lucia's stunt double Victoria Lee to reveal who played Jason.

"After keeping my mouth shut for YEEAARRSSS (and what feels like FOREVER!!!), I can finally share that I've been lucky enough to help bring Lucia to life as her main stunt double in Grand Theft Auto 6, along with a whole bunch of other characters stunts along the way!" Lee wrote in a picture of her and Manni, and rumoured Jason actor Dylan Rourke, on Instagram.

"A special shoutout to Manni and Dylan! You two are truly amazing humans, inside and out! So much talent, heart, and genuine goodness. I'm forever grateful to have shared this wild ride with you both!" she added.

And Rockstar's official cast list for GTA 6 confirms that yes, it is Dylan Rourke who plays the role.

A post shared by Victoria Lee (@victoria_lee_stunts).

Rourke's own Instagram account doesn't feature any news of his involvement in GTA 6, but his name was referenced in a recent IGN Holland article, as spotted on Reddit, earlier today.

Stephen Root, who plays Brian Heder, was the only actor to confirm his involvement in GTA 6 prior to the game's release, though it's a name many people had already guessed following the game's Netflix extended look.

Tech Report: Alt Video is a digital, faux Blockbuster video store that you can fill with movies from your Letterboxd watchlist and Plex server

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (479 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since the beginning of the year, I have watched almost 150 films.
  • According to recent reports, this is, obviously, not so dissimilar to Boxroom, a game where you can design your own bedroom that lets you use your Steam profile to fill it with games you actually own.
  • Alternatively, and perhaps more enticingly, if you run something like a Plex or Jellyfin server, you can hook that up to the game too, where again all of the films you own digitally show up in store.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since the beginning of the year, I have watched almost 150 films. I know this, because over the past few years, I've become one of those people… a Letterboxd user. Gasp! I know, I know, but I don't think I'm too insufferable about it. I'll only do a joke review in the hopes of like farming if I think it's genuinely funny! But many of these films were watched digitally, meaning I don't have a bunch of DVDs to admire on a shelf. So what am I to do? Well, I could check out Alt Video, a not quite job simulator where you can use your Letterboxd account or media server to fill up a digital, faux Blockbuster.

According to recent reports, this is, obviously, not so dissimilar to Boxroom, a game where you can design your own bedroom that lets you use your Steam profile to fill it with games you actually own. With Alt Video, you do things slightly differently just because of the focus on a different format. So, say you have a Letterboxd account. After exporting some data from your account, you can bring that into Alt Video, and this fake video store will then get filled up with shelves of DVD cases of all the films you've watched.

Alternatively, and perhaps more enticingly, if you run something like a Plex or Jellyfin server, you can hook that up to the game too, where again all of the films you own digitally show up in store. What's more interesting here is that there's a cinema room in the store that lets you watch films on your Plex server, and it's possible to invite your Steam friends to watch along with you. There's even a few other rooms, like a '90s bedroom or family room for more of a CRT kinda vibe. It's cute! If you like you can even manually add any DVDs or Blu-rays you own to appear on all the shelves too.

According to recent reports, there's a lot of other nice touches too. In the case of your Letterboxd data, your ratings even show up on the back of the boxes. It's not just relegated to films either, you can put in reveals or even your games. The whole thing can be played in VR if you really want that immersive feel. There's a store clerk who can give you some recommendations if you're not sure what to watch. And there's even a day and night system, weather, and seasonal shopfront facelifts.

Recent findings suggest that alt Video is currently slated for release next week on November 24th, and it'll be doing so in early access. Worth noting that for now the focus is on the browsing, but features involving serving customers and running the store are on the way. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.
